summary:
FireWatch is an interactive web platform that lets anyone explore more than two decades of fire hotspot activity in Mexico, using NASA FIRMS data from the MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors.

The two sensors detect fires at different resolutions, so their raw data cannot be compared directly over time. We built a backend that cleans and harmonizes both sources into one consistent historical record from 2000 to today. On top of it, we built a map-first web app: users draw a rectangle over any region and instantly get key indicators, a months-by-years calendar heatmap, the annual trend, and how the selected year compares with the historical median. A comparison view shows the same area in two different years side by side, and recurrent wildfire zones are highlighted directly on the map. Results can be exported as CSV or as an interpretive PDF report, in English or Spanish.

Wildfires in Mexico follow seasonal and geographic patterns that are hard to see in raw satellite data. FireWatch turns that data into clear, comparable evidence, helping researchers, authorities, and communities identify where and when fire activity concentrates, and plan prevention efforts accordingly.
details:
FireWatch is a web platform for exploring the history of fire activity in Mexico from 2000 to 2025, built on NASA FIRMS data from the MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) sensors.

Users start with a map of Mexico showing hotspots for the most recent year. They can click and drag to draw a rectangle over any region, and the platform immediately shows: total fire activity, the most active year and months, the change compared with the historical median, a calendar heatmap (months by years) with the selected year highlighted, and the annual trend with historical peaks. Recurrent wildfire zones are painted directly on the map. A Compare view shows the same area in two years side by side, on the same color scale. Results can be downloaded as CSV or as a PDF report that includes the map, the charts, and a written interpretation of the findings.

Behind the interface is a data pipeline we built for this project. We processed 8.3 million raw FIRMS detections in four main steps:

1. Removing heat sources that are not fires. FIRMS detects any thermal anomaly, including volcanoes, refineries, and gas flares. We kept only vegetation fires, built a mask from MODIS to correct a known classification issue in VIIRS version 2 files, and added a persistence filter that identifies industrial sites by their temporal pattern: they burn all year, while real fires in Mexico concentrate in March to May.

2. Harmonizing the sensors. VIIRS (375 m) sees many more points than MODIS (1 km) for the same fire, so simply adding detections creates artificial jumps when new satellites launched in 2012 and 2018. We counted fire activity in a common unit, the 1 km "cell-day", and calibrated the MODIS-only years (2000-2011) with monthly factors measured over the 14 years when both sensors overlap. The result is a consistent 25-year series without sensor-driven steps.

3. Detecting recurrent zones. We identified areas of about 5.6 km that had significant fire activity in at least 15 of 25 years, using only MODIS because it is the only sensor available for the whole period. The result is 369 polygons covering 1.7% of Mexico.

4. Validation. The harmonized calendar reproduces Mexico's known fire season, and the historical peaks (2011, 2005, 2003) match documented extreme seasons.

BENEFITS

- Turns millions of raw satellite records into clear indicators that anyone can read, without GIS or programming skills.

- Makes years comparable across two decades, which is not possible with raw detection counts.

- Allows analysis of any region, from a whole state to a single valley, in seconds.

- Exports the underlying data (CSV) and a ready-to-share report (PDF) in English or Spanish.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want FireWatch to support fire prevention and planning in Mexico. Environmental authorities and civil protection agencies can see where fires recur and when the season peaks in their region, to plan resources and prevention campaigns. Researchers get a harmonized, documented dataset. Communities and journalists can check whether a fire season is unusual compared with the historical record.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Data: NASA FIRMS archive data (MODIS Collection 6, VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20).

- Data processing: Python, pandas, Jupyter Notebooks.

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, Shapely, pytest.

- Frontend: TypeScript, Vue 3, PrimeVue, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL (maps), ECharts (charts), vue-i18n, jsPDF.

- Infrastructure: Docker, Microsoft Azure (Container Apps, Static Web Apps), GitHub.

- No special hardware was used.

CREATIVITY

Most fire viewers show raw points for recent days. FireWatch focuses on long-term history and makes it comparable. Our main contributions are the cross-sensor harmonization, the persistence filter that separates industrial heat sources from real fires using only their temporal pattern, and recurrent zones shown directly on the map. The PDF report goes beyond exporting charts: it includes a written interpretation of the selected area.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: every threshold is derived from the data and documented, including its limitations. The 2000-2011 values depend on a calibration factor, comparisons with few detections are flagged as unreliable, and colors represent activity levels, not fire risk.

- Data quality: we manually checked the most active cells against satellite imagery to confirm they were fires and not industrial sites.

- Accessibility: a color scale readable in light and dark mode, legends on every chart, and information that never depends on color alone.

- Audience: a bilingual interface (English and Spanish), since the main users are in Mexico.

- Attribution: we acknowledge NASA FIRMS, LANCE, and ESDIS as the source of the data.
